title: Writing the replication note
objectives: Write a plain note on how much of the effect survived.

screens.title: How much survived
screens.prose: The note this lesson writes replicates Jegadeesh and Titman (1993), "Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers" (JT). Its key line answers the curriculum's question: how much of the effect survived after publication?

rows: Alpha on market and four factors (t)

state.caption: The replication's results, seeded panel; % a month.

screens.question: Before 1990 the 6/6 skip spread was 1.04%; after, 0.27%. What share survived?

hints.text: Survival is after divided by before.
About 26%.

byKey.decl: You gave the share lost. Survival is after over before.

explain.text: 0.27 / 1.04 ≈ 26%: about a quarter of the effect survived. The decline is about three quarters. Both need the t of −1.28 beside them.

screens.title: A draft note
screens.prose: Here is a colleague's draft summary. Every number is right. One line claims more than the data can show.

lines: This proves momentum is a real anomaly.
Cohort returns: Newey-West t 3.59 with 5 lags.
Alpha 1.02% a month after five exposures.
Worst month −25.4%, a rebound after a bear market.
Net of 25 bp a side: 0.82% a month.

screens.question: Tap the line that overclaims.

hints.text: Which line is a conclusion, not a number?
Our panel was planted.
Line 3 claims the anomaly is real.

feedback.correct: Correct. A planted panel proves nothing about markets.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the line that draws a conclusion the panel cannot support.

byKey.l6: That line reports the extension with its t. It is honest.
byKey.l2: That line reports a number with its t. It is honest.

explain.text: Line 3 turns a match on planted data into a claim about markets. Every other line reports a number with its method. Lesson 6 said why: we put the effect in ourselves.

screens.title: The replication note
screens.prose: The **replication note** is one page. It runs from the question, the paper and the data, through method and the main table. Then come errors, risk, the extension, crashes and costs. It ends with what failed and what changes on real data.

screens.question: Which section tells a reader how far to trust the numbers on real markets?

options.text: What changes on real data
The main table
options.why: The table reports our numbers; it cannot say how they would differ on CRSP.

options.text: Method
options.why: Method says what we did, not how real data would change it.

options.text: Costs
options.why: Costs are one of the real-data issues, not the whole section.

hints.text: Which section talks about CRSP and free data?
It is near the end.
"What changes on real data".

feedback.correct: Correct. That paragraph is the one this course owes you.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which section compares our panel with real markets?

explain.text: Our panel was built to show the paper's effect. The real-data section lists what a CRSP or free-data run would face. Without it a reader cannot tell a code test from evidence.

screens.title: The survival sentence
screens.prose: The note's key sentence reports the extension.

rows: Alpha on market and four factors (t)

state.caption: The replication's results, seeded panel; % a month.

screens.question: Which sentence is honest?

options.text: About a quarter survived (0.27% against 1.04%). 180 months cannot pin the decline down, and the decay was planted
The effect survived publication intact
options.why: You ignored a 74% decline.

options.text: Momentum died after publication
options.why: You overclaimed from t 0.57: the data cannot rule out a moderate effect.

options.text: Exactly 26.4% of the effect survived
options.why: You gave false precision. The decline's standard error is wide.

hints.text: Which sentence gives a size with its uncertainty?
It also names the planted decay.
Only one says all three.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The sentence needs the size, its uncertainty and what the panel plants.

explain.text: About a quarter survived, but the standard error is wide and the decay was our choice. Saying "died" or "intact" claims more than 180 months allow. Exact decimals pretend to precision we do not have.

screens.title: What changes on real data
screens.prose: The real-data paragraph lists what a CRSP or free-data run would face. Hong, Lim and Stein (2000) found momentum stronger in small shares. Lesmond, Schill and Zhou (2004) argue costs absorb much of it.

rows: Alpha on market and four factors (t)

state.caption: The replication's results, seeded panel; % a month.

screens.question: Select all that apply: which belong in the paragraph?

options.text: Survivorship and missing delisting returns
A universe rebuilt point in time
Small, illiquid shares carrying much of the effect, with costs that eat it
The January effect in the losers
No generator to check against, and a noisier spread
Re-running with another seed of the generator
options.why: You listed a panel-only check. Real data has no seed to change.

hints.text: Which items exist only on real data?
A seed exists only on our panel.
Everything but the seed belongs.

feedback.correct: Correct. Five real-data issues; the seed is a panel tool.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep every issue a real dataset raises.

explain.text: Real data brings survivorship, point-in-time universes, small-share costs, the January effect and no known truth. The paper reports the losers' returns cluster in January, which our panel does not plant. A seed is how we measured noise here, not a real-data issue.

options.text: The out-of-sample extension, crashes and costs: how much survived and at what risk
Nothing: the table is the replication
options.why: You stopped at the in-sample match. The curriculum's exit asks how much survived out of sample.

options.why: More in-sample cells answer the same question again.

options.why: Picking the best seed is snooping.

hints.text: What does the exit ask for?
An extension and how much survived.
The table alone gives neither.

feedback.correct: Correct. An in-sample match is half a replication.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does the curriculum's exit ask?

byKey.none: You took the table as the whole note. The extension is what the course exit asks for.

explain.text: The exit asks for an out-of-sample extension and how much survived. The table only shows our code matches the paper on planted data. The extension, crash and cost lines show what a trader would actually get.

screens.title: When nothing survives
screens.prose: Suppose your extension found −0.10% a month after 1990, t −0.2.

rows: Alpha on market and four factors (t)

state.caption: The replication's results, seeded panel; % a month.

screens.question: How should the note report it?

options.text: State it plainly: none of the effect survived on this test, with the t and the caveats
Leave the extension out and report the in-sample table
options.why: You hid a result because it disappointed. That is the bias the course warns about.

options.text: Try other splits until some effect appears
options.why: You searched for a better answer. The split comes from the paper.

options.text: Announce that momentum is dead
options.why: A t of −0.2 cannot rule out a small positive effect either.

hints.text: Is a null result worth reporting?
Yes, with its standard error.
Never tune the split to rescue it.

feedback.correct: Correct. A null result is a result.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Report what you found, with its uncertainty.

explain.text: A failed extension is information: it belongs in the note with its t. Hiding it or tuning the split would bias every reader. The survival function below handles it with "None of the effect survived".

screens.title: The note in order
screens.prose: Put the note's sections in the order a reader needs them. The two robustness sections, standard errors and risk, may come either way round.
screens.question: Order the sections.

lines.text: Question, the paper and its claim
Data: the seeded panel, what it plants, why
Main table against the paper's quoted cells
Risk: alpha on the market and factors
What failed, and what changes on real data

hints.text: A reader needs the question and data first.
Results come after method; robustness after the table.
The real-data caveats close the note.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each section needs the ones before it.

explain.text: Question, data and method let a reader check the table. Standard errors and risk test it, then the extension, crashes and costs. The real-data paragraph says how far it all carries.

screens.title: The survival line in code
screens.prose: Turn the two means into the note's sentence. A negative or zero survival reads "None of the effect survived". With no in-sample effect there is nothing to survive.

screens.question: Write `survival_ratio(pre, post)` returning `(ratio, sentence)`, the ratio rounded to 4 places. Raise `ValueError` if `pre <= 0`.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests, including a negative, a zero, a growing effect and a zero in-sample mean.

hints.text: Check pre ≤ 0 first and raise.
Then compute post / pre.
`f"{round(100 * ratio)}% of the effect survived"` for a positive ratio.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Handle pre ≤ 0 first, then ratio ≤ 0, then the percentage.

explain.text: For our numbers, 0.0027 / 0.0104 gives 26%. A negative ratio means none survived, not a negative share. A ratio above 1, such as 120%, is allowed: effects can grow.

screens.title: The README and the interview
screens.prose: Your GitHub replication is done. An interviewer asks: "Tell me about your replication in two sentences."

rows: Alpha on market and four factors (t)

state.caption: The replication's results, seeded panel; % a month.

screens.question: Which answer is best?

options.text: I rebuilt Jegadeesh and Titman's 6/6 strategy and matched their 0.95% within 0.1 se on a planted panel. Out of sample about a quarter survived, with a −25% crash month and 0.82% net of costs
I proved momentum works and earns 1% a month
options.why: You claimed evidence from a planted panel and ignored the extension.

options.text: I did a project on momentum using Python
options.why: You gave no result. Name what you reproduced and what survived.

options.text: I used NumPy, statsmodels and Newey-West errors
options.why: You listed tools. The interviewer wants the finding.

hints.text: Which answer gives numbers and caveats?
It has the match, the survival and the risk.
Only one does all three.

feedback.correct: Correct. What you did, what matched, what survived, at what risk.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Two sentences: the match, then the survival and the risk.

explain.text: The best answer names the paper, the match and its basis, then the survival, the crash and the costs. It is honest that the panel was planted. That is the curriculum's exit in two sentences.

ideas: The note answers how much survived: about a quarter on our panel (0.27% against 1.04%), with its uncertainty.
Every number goes in with its method; the planted panel tests code, not markets.
The real-data paragraph lists survivorship, point-in-time universes, small-share costs, January and no known truth.

formula.name: Survival
formula.note: Report with the t of the difference; none if the ratio is not positive.

summary.trap: A note that stops at the in-sample table.

quiz.question: What share of the effect survived?

byKey.decl: You gave the decline. Survival is after over before.

explain.text: 0.60 / 0.80 = 75% survived; the decline is 25%. Report it with the t of the difference. That decides whether the decline is distinguishable from noise.

quiz.question: Which line belongs in a replication note on our seeded panel?

options.text: The panel plants the effect, so the match tests our code
The match proves momentum exists
options.why: A planted panel cannot be evidence about markets.

options.text: Our best cell earns 1.35% a month
options.why: Quoting the best of 32 cells is cell-picking.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which line is honest about the data?

explain.text: The panel was built to show the effect. So matching it tests the machinery only. The note must say so.

quiz.question: Which paper argued that trading costs absorb much of momentum's profit?

options.text: Lesmond, Schill and Zhou (2004)
Hong, Lim and Stein (2000)
options.why: They found momentum stronger in small shares.

options.text: McLean and Pontiff (2016)
options.why: They measured post-publication declines across anomalies.

explain.text: Lesmond, Schill and Zhou (2004) argue costs eat much of the strategy's profit. Hong, Lim and Stein (2000) found it stronger in small shares, where costs are highest. Both belong in the real-data paragraph.
